items.title: Brazil court places Bolsonaro under house arrest on health grounds

featured_image.name: Brazil court places Bolsonaro under house arrest on health ...

items.description:
Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ruled on Tuesday to place former President Jair Bolsonaro under house arrest on health grounds, reversing months of denied requests from the right-wing leader's legal team, according to Reuters.[1]

Bolsonaro, 71, has been serving a 27-year prison sentence since November for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. The house arrest will last for an initial 90-day period, after which Moraes said conditions will be reassessed. "The presence of the requirements necessary for maintaining humanitarian house arrest will be reassessed, including a medical examination if needed," the justice wrote in the decision.[1]

items.title: Israeli airstrike hits Christian town north of Beirut for first time

featured_image.name: Airstrike hits Lebanese Christian town north of Beirut ...

items.description:
An Israeli airstrike struck the Christian town of Sahel Alma north of Beirut on Tuesday, marking the first time the area had been targeted in the expanding war between Israel and Hezbollah, according to Lebanese state media and Reuters. There were no immediate reports of casualties, but witnesses told Reuters they heard several blasts and saw white smoke rising from the town.[1][2][3]

The strike represents a widening of Israel's air campaign into areas previously untouched by the conflict, which has killed more than 1,000 people in Lebanon and displaced over one million since fighting escalated on March 2.[4][5]

items.title: Iran charges ships up to $2M for Hormuz passage

featured_image.name: Iran War: Tehran Charges Some Ships Hormuz Transit Fees for Safe Passage -  Bloomberg

items.description:
Iran has begun levying transit fees of up to $2 million per voyage on some commercial vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz, effectively creating an informal toll on the world's most critical maritime energy chokepoint, according to Bloomberg.[1]

The payments are being sought on an ad hoc basis and do not appear to be systematic, people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. Some ships have already made the payment, though the mechanism and currency used remain unclear. Iranian authorities have officially denied that a formal policy exists, calling the reports "unfounded".[2][1]

items.title: US airstrikes kill 15 Iraq PMF fighters, including Anbar commander

featured_image.name: Airstrikes in Iraq on Iran-backed paramilitary alliance kill ...

items.description:
Airstrikes attributed to the United States and Israel killed at least 15 fighters from Iraq's Popular Mobilization Forces and wounded 30 others in western Iraq early Tuesday, in the deadliest single attack on the Iran-backed militia coalition since the US-Israeli war on Iran began in late February.

The strikes hit a PMF command headquarters in Iraq's Anbar province during a security meeting attended by senior commanders, according to Reuters. Among the dead was Saad al-Baiji, the PMF's operations commander for Anbar province. The PMF confirmed his death along with 14 of his companions in a statement posted on social media, calling the attack "a treacherous American targeting that struck the operations headquarters".[1][2]

items.title: Netanyahu taps top aide Dermer to vet US-Iran deal

featured_image.name: Netanyahu Taps Ron Dermer to Oversee US-Iran Deal Talks for Israeli  Interests - Bloomberg

items.description:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu assigned his closest confidant, former Strategic Affairs Minister Ron Dermer, to monitor US-Iranian negotiations and ensure Israel's core interests are not sacrificed in any potential deal to end the war, according to Bloomberg, citing an Israeli official speaking on condition of anonymity.[1][2]

Dermer's primary focus is on ensuring the dismantlement of Iran's nuclear program and the removal and elimination of roughly 440 kilograms of highly enriched uranium — material that Iran reportedly boasted to White House Special Envoy Steve Witkoff was sufficient for 11 nuclear bombs, according to Jewish Insider.[3]

items.title: Trump claims Iran gave US an energy 'present' tied to Hormuz

featured_image.name: Trump: 'Major points of agreement' with Iran after talks

items.description:
President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that Iran had made a major energy-related concession to the United States, describing it as a gift that "arrived today" — though he offered no specifics and Iran has repeatedly denied engaging in any negotiations with Washington.

"They gave us a present and the present arrived today, and it was a very big present, worth a tremendous amount of money," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, according to Reuters. "It wasn't nuclear; it was oil-and-gas-related, and it was a very nice thing they did."[1]

Trump said the gesture was connected to the Strait of Hormuz, the critical waterway through which roughly 20% of the world's oil supply passes. He characterized it as proof that "we're dealing with the right people" in Tehran and claimed Iran had also agreed it "will never have a nuclear weapon," The Independent reported.[2][3]

items.title: Iran refuses talks with Witkoff and Kushner, eyes Vance

featured_image.name: JD Vance is walking a tightrope on Iran. What does he really think?

items.description:
Iran has refused to continue diplomatic engagement with President Donald Trump's top envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, accusing them of deception in the lead-up to the U.S.-Israeli strikes that began on February 28, according to The Telegraph. Gulf sources told the publication that Tehran now views Vice President JD Vance as its preferred American interlocutor, owing to his well-documented skepticism of military intervention abroad.[1][2]

The shift comes as mediating nations work to arrange a potential meeting in Islamabad, Pakistan, that could bring together Vance and Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf as early as this week.[3][4]

items.title: Denmark's left bloc wins election but falls short of majority

featured_image.name: Exit polls: Frederiksen's Social Democrats win Danish election but probably  no majority

items.description:
Denmark's left-wing bloc led by Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen emerged ahead in Tuesday's parliamentary election but failed to secure a governing majority, with the Social Democrats posting their weakest result in 125 years and leaving centrist Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen positioned as kingmaker in what promises to be weeks of coalition negotiations.

With nearly all votes counted late Tuesday, the "red bloc" of left-leaning parties captured 84 seats in Denmark's 179-seat Folketing, while the right-wing "blue bloc" secured 77 seats — both well short of the 90 needed for a majority. Rasmussen's centrist Moderates, which won 14 seats, now hold the balance of power.[1][2]
